title: Why does Hollywood come to Berkshire?
content:
Travelling along the M4 near Junction 11, just outside Shinfield near Reading, you cannot miss a vast complex of grey buildings.
From the outside, they may not look particularly exciting, but behind their walls some of the world's biggest film and television productions are being made.
Shadowbox Studios Shinfield, in Wokingham, has 18 state-of-the-art sound stages, including two with more than 40,000 sq ft of floor space each.
The BBC goes behind the scenes to discover what has been filmed there and why the studios are important to the area.
The scale of the sound stages is immediately apparent. During his visit, BBC Radio Berkshire's Rich Clarke noted they were large enough for lorries to be reversed inside.
Studio operations manager Ruby Hornsey says it is "one of the largest stages in the UK and one of the largest in Europe".
Despite the busy motorway running nearby, she says the soundproofing means traffic cannot be heard inside, while noise from filming does not escape.
That allows the stages to be transformed into "many different worlds" for productions ranging from action thriller Greenland 2: Migration to the second series of Netflix's Squid Game: The Challenge.
The stages also have climate controls, allowing productions to alter the temperature to suit filming.
"For Squid Game: The Challenge they wanted one of the challenges to be quite warm in the room to make contestants a little bit more uncomfortable," Hornsey says.
"So we whacked up the heating in here to make the tensions higher."
Since opening in 2024, the studios have hosted a string of major film and television productions, including Avengers: Doomsday, Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire and Squid Game: The Challenge.
The Acolyte was another major production filmed there, with the studios describing the Star Wars series as a "huge milestone" requiring extensive soundstage space for its elaborate sets.
For sales manager Gemma McKeon, working alongside some of the biggest names in the industry is one of the perks of the job.
"It's one part of the job you're pinching yourself, especially when you get to see or sometimes, if you're lucky enough, meet your idols and the people that you've grown up watching," she says.
She says one of the most recent productions filmed there was Ebenezer, a comedy-drama starring Johnny Depp and Rupert Grint, which is due to be released in cinemas on 13 November.
McKeon says producers tend to consider three main factors when deciding where to film: the availability of skilled workers, financial incentives and studio facilities.
She says the UK is particularly strong in all three, while its variety of landscapes and historic locations also makes it attractive for shoots.
The figures suggest the UK's film and television industry is continuing to grow. British Film Institute (BFI) data show spending on film and high-end television production reached £6.8bn in 2025, up 22% on the previous year's initially reported figure.
The UK box office also generated £996.8m in 2025, a 2% increase on 2024.

title: A Court of Splintered Harmony: Why the latest mega-hit ACOTAR romantasy is dividing readers
content:
Sarah J Maas's blockbuster series is full of brutal wars, scheming faeries and spicy sex scenes. Now the sixth book in the saga is breaking sales records – and dividing opinion. What's the appeal? And is the latest novel actually any good?
Sarah J Maas is known as the "titan" of romantasy.
The subgenre, which is a blend of romance and fantasy, has become a dominating force in the world of fiction.
Its explosion in popularity, particularly among women under the age of 35, saw an estimated $610m worth of romantasy books sold in the US in 2024, and its popularity helped push UK overall fiction sales to more than £1bn that year.
The boom has been significantly driven by BookTok, a section of TikTok dedicated to book commentary, that has transformed the publishing industry. And BookTok was integral to the success of Maas's series, A Court of Thorns and Roses (also known as ACOTAR). Although the first novel was published in 2015, it saw massive viral success in 2020, which "really skyrocketed it into the stratosphere," says Dr Jodi McAlister, senior lecturer in Writing, Literature and Culture at Deakin University, Australia. "It was the snowball that started the modern romantasy avalanche rolling."
Since 2012, the US author has churned out a whopping 17 books across three romantasy series, the realms of which are all linked under a broader "Maasiverse" or Maas universe: Throne of Glass, ACOTAR and Crescent City. Together they have sold more than 100 million copies worldwide.
And on 27 October, after a five-year wait, fans descended on bookshops across the world for the much-anticipated release of the sixth book in the ACOTAR saga, A Court of Splintered Harmony. The book is tracking to be the largest book release of the year – it sold 1.7 million copies on the release date alone – a 600% increase on the fifth book, A Court of Silver Flames.
The series is undoubtedly Maas's most famous work and "inarguably the lynchpin of the modern romantasy boom," McAlister tells the BBC.
Here's what the ACOTAR books are about – and why readers love romantasy.
Firstly, some important historical context. Five hundred years before ACOTAR begins, humans had been enslaved by the fae (fairies), until a great seven-year war freed them, and a treaty was signed. The tension of land borders and the mortal-fae balance of power persist throughout the series.
Our story begins in the mortal lands, where we meet a 19-year-old human woman, Feyre Archeron, who is out hunting for food to bring back to her father and two older sisters. But things go awry as she ends up being dragged through a magical barrier known as The Wall, which separates the mortal lands from the faerie territory of Prythian.
When Feyre, who is a recurring protagonist throughout the series, passes into Prythian, what ensues is a turbulent journey through an ancient world with elaborate laws of magic, mystical and horrifying creatures, spicy sex and romance (derided by critics of the genre as "faerie smut"), villains and, of course, devastating wars.
Maas's world building is complex, with intricate plotlines that are not always resolved within one book. (Luckily there is a wealth of dedicated Reddit threads and even an ACOTAR wiki page to turn to.)
The author also uses different narrators to give readers an insight into other major characters – as well as Feyre's voice. This means that Maas has fleshed out ACOTAR's world even more, while keeping readers engaged and invested in their favourites. And of course, as fans conspire, the absence of a character's point of view may be a hint of a future plotline.
The origins of romantasy are centuries-old , so how did it become a multi-million-dollar subgenre?
Romantasy is mostly written by and for women, and centres around female protagonists.
This combines with key tropes like "fated mates" (a narrative device used to show that two characters are predestined to be together) and "forbidden love" against a backdrop of dark, magical worlds. The result is a perfect escape for young women and their desires. "While it's liberally populated with brooding, mysterious men, they're ultimately the love interests: female characters are regularly the protagonists and heroes," McAlister says.
But it also provides comfort.
"The great promise of the romance is that everything will turn out all right in the end," says McAlister. "And when you don't have that promise in your real life, the allure in fiction is powerful. We might be post-pandemic now, but we're still living in an uncertain world, and so romance's – and romantasy's – great promise remains deeply attractive."
This is a contentious question.

title: ITV Wales plans to cut programmes and jobs
content:
ITV Wales plans to cut two programmes and reduce the number of producer roles in its Cardiff headquarters.
The broadcaster said the proposals would "help to ease some cost pressure" and would allow its English language teams to "work more flexibly".
ITV confirmed it was proposing to end its long-running Coast and Country show and weekly arts and entertainment programme Backstage.
The changes would not affect the amount of news and current affairs programmes which are broadcast by ITV Wales each week.
A spokesperson said the broadcaster had begun consulting with staff after informing most of them about the proposals on Tuesday morning.
Coast and Country has run for over a decade and focuses on rural communities, the environment and the Welsh countryside.
It has been presented by weather presenter Ruth Dodsworth and Sean Fletcher.
BBC Wales understands that the number of producers working at ITV Wales may reduce from six to two as part of the restructure, while efforts to reduce expenditure could mean more programmes are made in the studio rather than on location.
An ITV Cymru Wales spokesperson said the wider industry was under "significant economic pressure" and these proposals were part of efforts to mitigate some of that financial strain.
They added that its plan to "restructure some of the teams that make our English language programmes to enable us to work more flexibly" while protecting its commitments to audience and the regulator, Ofcom.
Earlier this year, Sky agreed a £1.6bn deal to buy ITV's broadcasting and streaming operations, while leaving ITV Studios as a separate company. The takeover is subject to scrutiny , and may not proceed until late 2027.
In September BBC Wales announced it would cut 58 jobs as part of wider efforts across the BBC to save £500 million.
